items.title: pH 1 to pH 2 is a tenfold change, not a small one
items.claim: The pH scale runs from 0 to 14 and looks linear. It isn't. pH is the negative logarithm of [H+]. Each step on the scale is a factor of 10 in hydrogen-ion concentration.
items.prompt: How much more acidic is stomach acid (pH 1) than pure water (pH 7)?
items.reveal:
pH = -log10[H+]. Stomach acid at pH 1 has [H+] = 0.1 M. Pure water at pH 7 has [H+] = 10 to the minus 7 M. The ratio is 10 to the 6 — a million.

This is why diluting a strong acid even tenfold barely changes its pH: the absolute concentration drops by a factor of 10, the pH only shifts by 1 unit.

The same logic applies to the Richter scale (earthquakes), decibels (sound intensity), and stellar magnitudes (brightness). Logarithmic scales let humans handle quantities spanning many orders of magnitude — but they hide the underlying spread.
items.why: Linear-looking scales can describe quantities ranging over 14 orders of magnitude. Acidity's arithmetic must respect the log.

items.title: An 18-year-old's failed antimalarial attempt founded the synthetic dye industry
items.claim: In 1856 William Henry Perkin, an 18-year-old chemistry student in London, was trying to synthesise the antimalarial quinine from coal tar. He failed. The black sludge he produced, when washed with alcohol, gave a brilliant purple solution. He had made mauveine — the first synthetic dye.
items.prompt: Why did Perkin's mauve change the world?

options.text: It launched the synthetic organic dye industry, which became the seedbed of pharmaceutical chemistry, plastics, photography and modern industrial chemistry — particularly in Germany

items.reveal:
Perkin was working in his home laboratory during the Easter holiday. The bench was a board across the bathtub. He oxidised aniline (from coal tar) with potassium dichromate and got a tarry mess. Cleaning the flask with alcohol, he noticed an intense purple solution.

He filed a patent (despite being a minor), set up a factory at age 19 with his father and brother, and made a fortune. Queen Victoria wore mauve to her daughter's wedding in 1858. The colour exploded across European fashion.

Germany rapidly built on the industry. By 1900 BASF, Hoechst, Bayer and Agfa dominated synthetic chemistry and were turning out hundreds of new dyes. Aspirin (Bayer, 1899) and Salvarsan (Ehrlich, 1909) came out of the same dye-research tradition.

Perkin retired wealthy at 36 to do pure research.
items.why: An accidental failure can found an entire industry. The dye industry seeded pharmaceutical chemistry and modern materials science.

items.title: Rust costs the world about 3 percent of global GDP every year
items.claim: The NACE International IMPACT study (2016) estimated the global cost of corrosion at 2.5 trillion US dollars per year — about 3.4 percent of global GDP. Bridges, ships, pipelines, vehicles, buildings: the world fights iron's tendency to oxidise.
items.prompt: What makes iron-based rust particularly destructive?

options.text: Iron oxide (Fe2O3) has greater volume than the iron it formed from, so it flakes off rather than forming a protective layer; underlying metal is constantly exposed, and the process continues until the structure fails
Iron rusts in a chain reaction

items.reveal:
When aluminium oxidises, Al2O3 has nearly the same molar volume as the metal, forming a tight, protective coating. When iron oxidises, hydrated Fe2O3 occupies more space than the metal, breaks free, flakes off, and exposes fresh iron to the next round.

The Pilling-Bedworth ratio for iron is about 2.1 (oxide volume vs metal volume). For aluminium it's about 1.3. A ratio close to 1 gives a protective layer; ratios much larger than 1 give flaking; ratios much smaller than 1 give porous, useless layers.

Protection strategies: galvanising (zinc sacrificial anode), painting (barrier coating), stainless-steel alloying with Cr (which forms protective Cr2O3), cathodic protection (applied voltage), and design choices to keep moisture off.
items.why: Rust is taught as 'iron + oxygen + water'. The economics and the engineering of corrosion control are vast.
